title: After AI Steals the Talent, Only Six Tokens Are Left to Own
dek: Delphi's Yan Liberman says crypto VCs make one deal a year because AI has sucked up all the smart people; the only things that can still make money are a handful of tokens with real revenue that don't depend on the crypto market.
why: A frontline crypto VC publicly shares his six positions and his reasoning, including why he no longer does crypto VC and why he has given up on the gaming vertical. High information density, but you need some crypto background.
who: Crypto fund managers, token investors, and practitioners who want to understand how a frontline crypto VC allocates capital and evaluates founders.
skip: The ad segment from 16:17 to 17:57 can be skipped.

points.h: This rally has no obvious buyer
points.body: Yan says the market was caught off guard by ‘QE in the form of long-end bond curve control’, triggering a short squeeze, but he personally finds it hard to see a new high in the short term, because it would require a lot of new money, and the obvious buyer historically (Sailor) isn't buying now — instead he's cashmaxing and paying down preferred stock. He thinks leverage hasn't built up excessively, and this sequence of slow grind, pause, alt rotation is actually healthy. Another structural change is that the alt market has gotten shallower, money concentrates more easily into a few assets, so you don't need a whole new cohort of buyers to move the market — it has become a ‘stock picker's market’.

points.h: Buy things that look like hot coins but aren't as crowded
points.body: Yan admits there are only about 10 to 15 investable liquid tokens right now, and every crypto fund is already positioned in those 15. His conclusion: you should look for names that ‘look and smell like these coins, but aren't as crowded in trading’. Hyperliquid is a long-term bull, but going to 200 in four months would be surprising; for short-term outperformance you have to look at less obvious names. Santi adds that with 15 investable coins, any liquid fund going on a show keeps naming the same five.

points.h: Crypto VC does one deal a year
points.body: Yan says of their newest venture fund's five investments, only one is crypto, and over the past year they did only one crypto VC deal. The reason is that crypto VC's value capture and defensibility are now clearer, so you can quickly filter out a large number of projects, but the thesis that ‘crypto gets broadly adopted across multiple verticals’ has been sidelined, and AI is a major factor in attracting talent, attention and capital. His only crypto investment is Tori Finance, a tokenized Turkish lira carry trade, USD-hedged, about 10.5% organic yield, no incentives.

points.h: The six tokens share one thing: revenue not tied to crypto
points.body: Yan's six public tokens are Hyperliquid, Zcash, Lighter, Venice, Grass, Aerodrome. He says he prefers projects with a ‘revenue story’ that aren't highly dependent on crypto activity, because that makes them more resilient and gives a stronger TAM story. He details Grass: projected $70 million revenue, $40 million operating profit, doing residential IP network data scraping, customers are frontier labs, token market cap $330 million, unlocks end in October, about 30% of supply in the foundation, no equity only the foundation, and if valued as a pure equity non-crypto business, the private market could probably raise $1 to 2 billion.

points.h: The return requirement for crypto has changed
points.body: Yan says he no longer anchors on annualized return rates, but instead sets individual price targets, stop losses and invalidation conditions, and keeps a reserve of money to handle a ‘total collapse’. He admits he just likes volatility. Santi says he now doesn't do crypto VC that can't at least 10x, Ethereum at $300 billion has no clean 10x, and the downside asymmetry is far greater than the upside. Yan responds that comfort comes from holding ‘productive assets’ rather than ‘reflexive assets’, and the key to a productive asset is the durability of its earnings and how much it depends on reflexive assets.

points.h: The gaming vertical has been abandoned
points.body: Yan says gaming as a whole is a hard vertical to invest in, because games as a business have too short a lifecycle, and once you run the NPV the long-term value story is hard to sustain. They tried Gunzilla, a big bet, and the result was bad; he attributes it to management and spending issues, not game quality — the game itself is AAA level, on par with Call of Duty, PUBG, Fortnite. He says this may be their last attempt at AAA level, and after that gaming as a broad category will be hard, with only small versions of games doing well. They now think the only truly investable vertical left is basically ‘financialized applications’.

points.h: Aerodrome is a classic catch-up trade
points.body: Yan says Aerodrome originally planned to migrate to mainnet in mid-July and support multiple chains, but it was delayed, hurting the price; now the launch is set for the second half of September, with migration to ETH and ARC announced, and whether it migrates to Robin Hood unconfirmed. He sees this as a huge opportunity for TVL, volume and fees, and many people treat it as a catch-up trade. The prior problem was the relationship between emissions and revenue — emissions go to LPs, revenue goes to stakers, criticized as using emissions to offset revenue. Now they want to make emissions dynamic, tied one-to-one to trading volume, so price up means emissions down; at the same time they are adding multiple revenue lines, estimated to contribute an extra 40% of revenue with no emissions offset. Currently OI relative to market cap is not a large position.

points.h: The investment committee now weighs founders most
points.body: Yan says if he could pick only one change, it's the weight of founder due diligence. In early crypto it was obvious what needed to exist, so investing was more by idea and defensibility, with lower founder weight. But once you go into other professional verticals, you can't really diligence the idea and moat, and the only repeatable, scalable thing is the founder side. They now ask ‘what is your earliest memory, then walk us through your life’. He also mentions the ‘chip on the shoulder’ from childhood trauma and the desperate desire to win as actually valuable factors, and gives Athena's Guy as an example, saying he will stop at nothing to win.
